region: The Levant: Mount Lebanon, the Bekaa Valley, Damascus, Aleppo and the Syrian interior
title: Lebanon and Syria — Cedars, Crusader Castles and the Road to Damascus
subtitle: A Levantine overland concept from the Qadisha Valley to Palmyra: cannot currently be recommended
summary: Qadisha Valley, Baalbek, Damascus's old city, Krak des Chevaliers and Aleppo make a rich overland concept, but every reviewed government advises against travel to Syria, and the Netherlands and the US advise against all travel to Lebanon.
introduction: The Levant packs more layers of history into a few hundred kilometres than almost anywhere. The imagined route would start in Beirut and Byblos, climb to the cedars and Qadisha Valley's cliff monasteries, then cross to Baalbek's Roman temples in the Bekaa. It would continue over the Masnaa crossing to Damascus's Umayyad Mosque and souks, north to the Hama waterwheels, Krak des Chevaliers and Aleppo's citadel, and out to Palmyra in the desert. It is shown as a geographical and cultural concept only. Official advice for both countries currently rules out recommending it, and no operational itinerary is offered.

exceptional.vsOman: Oman is empty space crossed by a self-driven tent trip; this concept is dense cities, castles and mountain monasteries, mostly with drivers and guides, and the opposite of independent: checkpoints, permits and advisories remove most freedom.
exceptional.vsPackageTourism: Few packages combine Lebanon and Syria; a link-up of Qadisha hiking, Baalbek and a Damascus-Aleppo-Palmyra loop would be distinctive, but today any real offer would be an operator-managed tour in a country where governments advise against travel.
exceptional.vsPortfolio: On cultural layering it would rival Jordan, Egypt or Iraq, and Crusader castles are unique within the portfolio. It cannot compete on eligibility, where Syria's blanket advice places it alongside Iraq as an excluded concept.

coordinates.label: Qadisha Valley / Bekaa, between the two countries

duration.note: Indicative only; the route is not operational. A 14-day concept would use about 5 days in Lebanon and 7 in Syria, plus two flight days.

recommendedTravelWindow.window: Mid to late March, if the route ever becomes feasible
recommendedTravelWindow.rationale: March is warmer and the Cedars and Qadisha are more reachable as snow melts, and Syria's interior (Palmyra) is mild; February is cold and wet and the cedar road is often snow-blocked. Ramadan until about 9 March would affect restaurants, so late March is better still. This is climate reasoning only, not a recommendation to go.

februarySuitability.summary: Cold, rainy and snowy at altitude: the cedars and upper Qadisha are often inaccessible, Ramadan starts about 8 February and Syrian interior nights are near freezing.

marchSuitability.summary: Mild at the coast and in Damascus, snow retreating from the cedar road by late March, and fewer rain days; Ramadan runs until about 9 March and Eid follows.

climate.regionNote: Mediterranean coast (mild, wet winter), Mount Lebanon (cold, snow above about 1,500 m), the Bekaa and Syrian interior (continental, cold nights) and the Palmyra desert (dry, cool winter). Figures are rounded climate normals for planning, not forecasts.

february.rainfall: Wettest part of the year on the coast and Mount Lebanon; frequent showers
february.humidity: Moderate to high on the coast
february.notes: Beirut about 16 C by day; Damascus 11-13 C by day and near 0-3 C at night; Bsharri and the cedars below freezing at night with snow cover.

march.rainfall: Declining; some rain days remain on the coast
march.notes: Beirut about 18-19 C; Damascus 16-18 C; Palmyra warm by day and cool at night; cedars still snowy early March, passable later.

climate.snowAndMountainAccess: The Cedars of God ski area and the Bsharri road are often snow-covered from December to March; walking in the upper Qadisha may need snowshoes and a local guide. Planning pattern, not verified for 2027.
climate.seaConditions: Mediterranean swimming is cold (about 17-19 C); not a swimming trip.
climate.airQuality: Beirut and Damascus have traffic and generator pollution; not a defining constraint.
climate.wildlifeSeasonality: Not a wildlife trip; cedars and spring wildflowers in March.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Ramadan
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Daytime restaurants and cafes are limited, especially in Syria; evenings are lively.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Domestic travel peaks, banks close, borders can be busy.

climate.ramadan2027: Expected about 8 February to 9 March 2027; Eid al-Fitr about 9-10 March. February is almost entirely Ramadan, with limited daytime dining and shorter opening hours, especially in Syria.
climate.lunarNewYear2027: Not relevant: Lunar New Year (6 February 2027) has no effect on this region.
climate.tourismDemand: Low and unpredictable. Lebanon's tourism has been disrupted by the 2026 conflict; Syria reports rising visitor numbers, many of them returning Syrians.
climate.flightPriceSeasonality: Fares to Beirut are moderate in winter outside holidays, but airspace closures and strikes have caused cancellations, so prices are unreliable.

geography.summary: Mount Lebanon rises over the coast to snowy peaks; the Qadisha gorge and the Bekaa lie behind, then the Anti-Lebanon range and Damascus, the Orontes valley, Aleppo's plateau and the Palmyra steppe.
geography.distinctive: The mix of snow-capped cedar forest, a deep monastery gorge and Syrian desert ruins in one overland sweep.

landscapes.name: Qadisha Valley and Cedars of God
landscapes.description: A cliff gorge with Maronite hermitages and the last high-altitude cedar groves.

landscapes.name: Bekaa Valley
landscapes.description: A broad farming plain between Mount Lebanon and the Anti-Lebanon range, home to Baalbek and wine country.

landscapes.name: Jeita Grotto
landscapes.description: A karst cave system with an underground river north of Beirut.

landscapes.name: Syrian steppe and Palmyra
landscapes.description: Open desert around the caravan city of Palmyra.

culture.summary: Phoenician, Roman, Byzantine, Crusader and Ottoman layers, living Christian, Sunni, Shia and Druze communities, and one of the Middle East's great food cultures.

culturalHighlights.name: Baalbek
culturalHighlights.description: Temples of Jupiter and Bacchus at one of the largest Roman sanctuaries.

culturalHighlights.name: Damascus old city
culturalHighlights.description: Umayyad Mosque, Straight Street and souks within the walls.

culturalHighlights.name: Krak des Chevaliers
culturalHighlights.description: A concentric castle on a hilltop above the Homs gap.

culturalHighlights.name: Lebanese table
culturalHighlights.description: Mezze, bakeries, and a long tradition of home cooking that can be experienced in family-run restaurants.

adventureHighlights.name: Qadisha Valley walking
adventureHighlights.description: Half-day to full-day walks between cliff monasteries; icy in winter.

adventureHighlights.name: Cedars in snow
adventureHighlights.description: Reaching the cedar grove in winter, possibly on snowshoes.

signatureExperiences.title: Walking the Qadisha Valley between cliff monasteries
signatureExperiences.description: A day on foot in the Holy Valley, past rock-cut hermitages and chapels, ending in Bsharri.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: One of the oldest continuous Christian monastic landscapes, in a gorge reachable in a day from the coast.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Local guide from Bsharri, a driver from Beirut or Byblos, and a check of snow and rain on the day.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Planning estimate for guide share and fees.

signatureExperiences.title: Damascus: Umayyad Mosque, souks and the old city at dusk
signatureExperiences.description: Two days in the walled city on foot, from the Umayyad Mosque to the Christian quarter and traditional bakeries.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: One of the oldest continuously inhabited capitals, walkable and largely intact.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Local guide, a hotel in the old city, and fresh security checks daily.

signatureExperiences.title: Baalbek's Roman sanctuary in the Bekaa
signatureExperiences.description: Half a day among the Temple of Bacchus and the Temple of Jupiter's six standing columns.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: The largest Roman temple platform in the empire's eastern provinces and exceptionally well preserved.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Hired driver from Beirut or Zahle; not possible while advice is against travel to the area.

signatureExperiences.title: Krak des Chevaliers and the Orontes valley
signatureExperiences.description: The Crusader fortress above Homs followed by the norias of Hama.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: The best-preserved medieval castle in the Middle East, combined with a working river-wheel town.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Syrian driver and guide; conditions on the Homs-Hama road must be checked.

travelStyle.summary: Hired driver and guide throughout, short hikes in the Qadisha and a land crossing at Masnaa.

transport.summary: A hired driver-with-vehicle is the realistic option: the Masnaa crossing is about 61 km from Beirut and 55 km from Damascus, and cars cannot be driven across freely. Intercity travel in Syria otherwise relies on drivers, since rail and domestic aviation are limited and unreliable.

modes.description: Daily rate in Lebanon; a Syrian driver and vehicle would take over across the border.
Beirut-Damascus shared taxis run through Masnaa; safety and reliability depend on the day's situation.
Qadisha Valley on foot with a local guide.

transport.carRental: Self-drive is not recommended. Cars rented in Lebanon generally cannot be taken into Syria, and the Netherlands warns of carjacking targeting rental cars in the Bekaa.

drivingRequirements.summary: Self-drive is not recommended: border, checkpoints, mines in some areas and carjacking reports.
drivingRequirements.internationalDrivingPermit: An IDP is advisable if a car is ever rented in Lebanon; Syria is not a self-drive destination.
drivingRequirements.licenceNotes: Two of the four hold car licences; neither would drive in Syria. A driver is used.
drivingRequirements.motorcycleNotes: No motorcycle or scooter riding without the required licence; none is planned.
drivingRequirements.recommendedApproach: Hired driver with a local guide, using licensed operators.

accommodation.summary: Guesthouses and mid-range hotels in Lebanon; hotels and boutique houses in Damascus and Aleppo's old cities. Available stock is limited and prices are volatile.

camping.summary: Camping is not recommended: unexploded ordnance, security and no established framework for foreign campers.

physicalDifficulty.label: moderate
physicalDifficulty.summary: Mostly cultural days; the Qadisha walks are the main exertion and are cold and slippery in February.

itinerary.summary: A conceptual outline of regions and themes only; it is not a bookable plan because the route requires areas under advice against all travel or all but essential travel.

overview.name: Beirut, Byblos and Jeita
overview.description: Beirut's corniche and neighbourhoods, Byblos's harbour and Jeita Grotto; the southern suburbs and the airport road are excluded by the FCDO.

overview.name: Qadisha Valley and the Cedars of God
overview.description: The monastery gorge and cedar grove above Bsharri, in snow in winter.

overview.name: Bekaa and Baalbek
overview.description: Roman temples; the area is under advice against all but essential travel.

overview.name: Lebanese south coast
overview.description: Sidon and Tyre, under advice against all travel in the South governorate.

overview.name: Damascus and Maaloula
overview.description: The old city and the Aramaic-speaking mountain village, reached over the Masnaa crossing.

overview.name: Hama, Krak des Chevaliers and Aleppo
overview.description: The norias, Crusader castle and Aleppo's partly restored old city.

overview.name: Palmyra and Bosra
overview.description: Desert ruins damaged in the war and a Roman basalt city in the south.

stops.name: Beirut Rafic Hariri International Airport
stops.description: Arrival and departure airport. The FCDO advises against all travel on Route 51 between central Beirut and the airport, so even reaching the capital by road is restricted.

stops.name: Beirut — Raouche corniche and downtown
stops.description: Cafes, bakeries and the sea-stack corniche. The southern suburbs (Dahiyeh) are separately under advice against all travel.

stops.name: Byblos (Jbeil)
stops.description: Phoenician, Roman and Crusader harbour town north of Beirut.

stops.name: Qadisha Valley and Bsharri
stops.description: Deep gorge with cliff monasteries, hiking and Kahlil Gibran's hometown.

stops.name: Cedars of God
stops.description: High grove of ancient cedars above Bsharri, snow-covered in winter.

stops.name: Baalbek
stops.description: Roman temple complex in the Bekaa. In an area under advice against all but essential travel.

stops.name: Sidon (Saida)
stops.description: Crusader Sea Castle and old souks; South governorate, against all travel.

stops.name: Masnaa border crossing
stops.description: Main Beirut-Damascus land crossing; closed and reopened during the 2026 war.

stops.name: Damascus old city
stops.description: Umayyad Mosque, souks and the old Christian quarter.

stops.name: Maaloula
stops.description: Mountain village where Western Aramaic is still spoken, damaged in the war.

stops.name: Krak des Chevaliers
stops.description: Crusader castle in the Homs governorate.

stops.name: Aleppo
stops.description: Citadel and souks, heavily damaged 2012-2016 and partly restored.

stops.name: Palmyra
stops.description: Desert caravan city, with monuments destroyed in 2015.

stops.name: Bosra
stops.description: Roman and Umayyad city with a black-basalt theatre, in Daraa governorate in the south.

stops.name: Tyre (Sour)
stops.description: Phoenician and Roman port with a hippodrome; South governorate, against all travel.

security.summary: Excluded: Syria is under advice against all travel or the equivalent from France, the UK, the Netherlands and the US, and Lebanon is red in the Netherlands, Level 4 in the US and largely discouraged by France and the UK for the south, Bekaa and Baalbek parts of the route.
security.assessedRoute: Beirut, Byblos, Qadisha Valley and the Cedars, Baalbek (Bekaa), the Masnaa crossing, Damascus, Maaloula, Hama, Krak des Chevaliers, Aleppo, Palmyra and Bosra, with Sidon and Tyre in the south considered as optional extras.

advisories.level: Travel formally discouraged across most of the country; orange zones discouraged except for compelling reasons (updated 10 Sep 2026; colour map not readable in text)
advisories.regionsAffected: Most of Lebanon; south under Israeli military operations; strikes possible in Beirut's southern suburbs

advisories.level: Travel discouraged; situation very unstable; terrorist threat very high across the country incl. Damascus (updated 10 Sep 2026)
advisories.routeImpact: The whole Syrian half is in the discouraged advice.

advisories.level: Against all travel: South and Nabatieh, Beirut southern suburbs and Route 51 to the airport, parts of Beqaa and northern Baalbek-Hermel; against all but essential travel: southern Mount Lebanon, southern Beqaa, rest of Baalbek-Hermel (updated 10 Aug 2026)
advisories.routeImpact: Baalbek and the airport road are covered; Sidon and Tyre are in the all-travel South.

conflictRisk.note: Israel-Hezbollah hostilities since 2 March 2026 with a June cessation of hostilities that has not stopped strikes in the south; Syria remains an unstable post-war state.

terrorismRisk.note: France rates the terrorist threat in Syria as very high including Damascus, citing the June 2025 church attack; the US cites terrorism for both countries.

kidnappingRisk.note: US advisories cite kidnapping and hostage-taking in both countries; the Netherlands reports kidnappings and arbitrary arrests in Syria.

regionalRestrictions: Smartraveller (Australia) could not be fetched; its level was not recorded.
Syria: no French, British, US or Dutch consular presence; the French consulate in Beirut covers emergencies.
Landmines and unexploded ordnance south of the Litani and in parts of Syria.
Carjacking of rental and expensive cars reported in the Bekaa (Netherlands advice).
ordinaryRisks: Winter snow and landslides on Mount Lebanon roads
security.medicalAccess: Beirut has good private hospitals; elsewhere in Lebanon and especially in Syria, healthcare is limited or unavailable, and evacuation is hard.
security.insuranceConsiderations: Standard travel insurance is generally void or excludes cover when travelling against government advice or into war zones; Canadian and US insurer notices list Lebanon and Syria as restricted. A specialist policy, if any, would need to be priced and read in full.
security.reassessmentRequired: Reassess if France, the UK and the Netherlands all lower their advice for the specific route, the Lebanon cessation holds, and a valid insurance policy exists. Recheck before any booking.

practicalRequirements.visa: Syria: visa on arrival reported for EU citizens (about USD 75 per third-party guides); the e-visa was not working in September 2026 and the rules (agency booking, pre-approval) shifted in November 2026, so a French citizen must check with a Syrian embassy. Lebanon: on-arrival entry for French citizens is expected but unverified.
practicalRequirements.entry: Entry to Lebanon after visiting Israel is refused; passport stamps from Syria may affect later travel to some countries.
practicalRequirements.passportValidity: Typically six months; check with each country.
permits: Syrian security permits for the desert and some historic sites (unverified)
practicalRequirements.insurance: Standard policies are unlikely to cover this route; see the security section.
practicalRequirements.connectivity: Lebanese SIMs are available; Syria has limited coverage and roaming is unreliable.
practicalRequirements.payments: Lebanon uses cash USD and the lira; Syria is largely cash, cards do not work.
practicalRequirements.medical: Carry a personal medical kit; evacuation insurance is difficult to obtain.

advantages: Unusual density of Phoenician, Roman, Crusader and Islamic heritage
Superb food and walkable old cities
Qadisha Valley and the cedars give a mountain contrast to the desert trips
disadvantages: Official advice against travel in Syria and across Lebanon in parts of the route
No standard insurance, no consular support in Syria
February is cold and mostly Ramadan; interior travel needs guides and permits
uncertainties: Whether the Israel-Hezbollah cessation of hostilities holds and what happens in the south and the Bekaa
Whether Syria's tourism rules (visa, agency requirement, permits) will be clarified
Whether any insurer will cover travel to either country
